titre: UBS Gives In to the United States, Then a Law Forces the Rest of the World
accroche: In 2009, Switzerland forces UBS to hand over the names of its American clients. In 2010, a law imposes the same transparency on every bank in the world.
contenu_vulgarise:
On February 18, 2009, UBS, Switzerland's largest bank, enters into a deferred prosecution agreement with the American justice system. The Department of Justice is prosecuting it for conspiring to defraud the United States by impeding the tax authority, the IRS, and presents the agreement as the admission of a bank that helped American taxpayers hide their accounts. UBS agrees to pay $780 million in fines, penalties, interest, and restitution. The Department calls another part of the agreement unprecedented: on the order of the Swiss financial regulator, FINMA, UBS hands the American government the identity of some of its American clients, along with information about their accounts.

The indictment describes a precise organization. Swiss bankers allegedly made about 3,800 trips to the United States in 2004 alone to talk to their clients about their Swiss accounts. Accounts were allegedly opened in the names of nominees or shell companies, so that the American taxpayer no longer appeared as the beneficial owner.

## A 30% Withholding to Persuade

Thirteen months later, on March 18, 2010, the law that generalizes this logic becomes public law. The provisions of FATCA (the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act) appear in Title V of a broader bill, the Hiring Incentives to Restore Employment Act, which became Public Law No. 111-147 on March 18, 2010. They are codified in Chapter 4 of the Internal Revenue Code, whose section 1471 sets out the mechanism.

This mechanism does not rely on direct coercion of the foreign bank. A foreign financial institution that has not entered into an agreement with the U.S. Treasury is subject to a 30% withholding on withholdable payments. The IRS states that an unregistered institution is generally subject to this withholding on the withholdable payments it receives, and that the withholding targets certain payments of U.S. source. To escape the withholding, the bank must therefore sign the agreement and commit to identifying which of its accounts are American, applying the required verification procedures, and reporting the specified information on those accounts every year. The 2010 text provided for application to payments made after December 31, 2012. In its questions and answers, the IRS sets June 30, 2014, as the date after which a withholding agent must obtain the identification number of a foreign institution for the payments it makes to it.

## The Shift

Read in hindsight, the 2010 law turns into general clauses what the UBS affair had obtained from a single bank. In 2009, UBS hands over the identities of American clients and commits to exiting the banking business with American clients who hold undeclared accounts. In 2010, the agreement that the text offers to all foreign banks contains the same substantive obligations: identify American accounts and report them every year. The text even anticipates the case of a local legal obstacle: when a foreign law would prevent a bank from reporting an account, the bank must try to obtain a waiver of that law from the account holder and, if it fails to do so within a reasonable time, close the account.

The sanction is not a prosecution but a condition of access: the agreement, or the 30% withholding on withholdable payments. The text leaves some exits open. The Treasury may treat as compliant an institution that shows, through procedures it prescribes, that it holds no American accounts, and the withholding does not apply to payments whose beneficial owner is a foreign government, an international organization, or a central bank of issue. A little over a year after the UBS affair, what was a bilateral negotiation under threat of prosecution becomes a choice imposed on every bank in the world: submit to reporting its American accounts, or accept that its payments of U.S. source will be cut by 30%.

repere.texte: On February 18, 2009, UBS agrees to pay $780 million and, on the order of the Swiss regulator, to hand over to the United States the identity of some of its American clients. On March 18, 2010, Public Law 111-147 establishes FATCA: a foreign bank that has not entered into an agreement with the U.S. Treasury is subject to a 30% withholding on withholdable payments.
repere.source: U.S. Department of Justice, UBS Enters into Deferred Prosecution Agreement, February 18, 2009; 26 U.S. Code § 1471 (Cornell LII)

carte.punch: UBS gives in to the United States in 2009. In 2010, a law offers the same deal to every bank.
carte.idee: In 2009, UBS hands over the names of some American clients on the order of the Swiss regulator and pays $780 million. In 2010, the FATCA law offers every foreign bank a reporting agreement, under penalty of a 30% withholding on withholdable payments.

quiz.question: What lever does the 2010 FATCA law use to push banks located outside the United States into an agreement with the American tax authority?
choix: By entrusting the Swiss FINMA with supervising every bank in the world
By relying on Interpol to criminally prosecute foreign banks that refuse to cooperate
By obtaining a UN resolution making the American law applicable everywhere
By withholding 30% of certain payments to banks that refuse an agreement with the Treasury
quiz.explication: The text does not provide for prosecuting the foreign bank: an institution that has not entered into an agreement with the U.S. Treasury is subject to a 30% withholding on withholdable payments, under 26 U.S.C. § 1471.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened on February 18, 2009, even before the FATCA law was passed?
choix: The U.S. Congress passes the first version of FATCA
UBS admits it helped clients hide their accounts and pays $780 million
A French bank is convicted for the same reasons as UBS
Switzerland permanently abolishes banking secrecy for all its clients
quiz_supplementaire.explication: UBS agrees to pay $780 million in fines, penalties, interest, and restitution, in an agreement the Department of Justice presents as the admission of a bank that helped American taxpayers hide their accounts.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On the order of which authority does UBS agree to hand over the identity of some of its American clients?
choix: The Swiss financial regulator
The U.S. Federal Reserve
The European Parliament
The International Monetary Fund
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is on the order of FINMA, the Swiss financial regulator, that UBS hands over the identity of some of its American clients, according to the Department of Justice press release.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which broader piece of legislation is the FATCA law included in 2010?
choix: The Dodd-Frank Act, a banking regulation law
The Patriot Act, a national security law
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act, a corporate accounting law
The HIRE Act, an employment law
quiz_supplementaire.explication: FATCA appears in Title V of the Hiring Incentives to Restore Employment Act, which became Public Law No. 111-147 on March 18, 2010.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What must a foreign bank bound by the FATCA agreement do if a law of its own country prevents it from reporting an American account?
choix: Try to obtain a waiver of that law from the account holder and, failing that, close the account
Report the account anyway and pay a fine to its own country
Transfer the account to an American bank without informing the holder
Ask the IRS to waive the reporting of that account
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Under 26 U.S.C. § 1471(b)(1)(F), the bank must try to obtain a valid waiver of the foreign law from the account holder and, if it does not obtain one within a reasonable time, close the account.
